::: {.callout-note}
## What this tutorial is about

For the rest of the course you will not plot *toy* spectra — you will
compute turbulence statistics from a **real direct numerical simulation
(DNS)** of homogeneous isotropic turbulence. This page sets the scene:
where the data comes from, how it was produced, where it lives on the
cluster, and what file format it is stored in. The hands-on work follows
in the assignment notebooks.
:::

## Where the data comes from

The velocity fields you will analyse are a subset of the **forced isotropic
turbulence** dataset from the **Johns Hopkins Turbulence Databases
(JHTDB)** — an open "simulation laboratory" that stores entire
space–time histories of large turbulence simulations and serves them to
anyone [@li2008; @perlman2007]. Instead of re-running an expensive DNS,
researchers query the stored fields directly, which is exactly what we do
here.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Acknowledgement

This dataset is provided by the **Johns Hopkins Turbulence Databases

### How it was computed: forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence

**Homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT)** is the simplest conceptual
setting for turbulence: the statistics are the same at every point
(homogeneous) and in every direction (isotropic). There are no walls, no
mean shear, and no preferred orientation — which makes it the canonical
test case for the theory you meet in lectures (the energy cascade, the
$-5/3$ Kolmogorov spectrum, the Taylor microscale).

The JHTDB field was produced by a **direct numerical simulation** — the
Navier–Stokes equations are solved *without any turbulence model*, so every
scale of motion from the largest eddies down to the dissipative
(Kolmogorov) scale is resolved on the grid. The essentials:

- **Method — pseudo-spectral.** Spatial derivatives are evaluated in
  Fourier space on a triply **periodic** cube of side $2\pi$, using a
  $1024^3$ grid (about $10^9$ points per snapshot). Pseudo-spectral schemes
  are the standard choice for isotropic DNS because periodic boundaries fit
  a box with no walls and because spectral derivatives are essentially
  exact.
- **Forcing keeps it stationary.** Real turbulence decays as it dissipates
  energy. To hold the flow *statistically steady*, energy is continuously
  injected at the **large scales** (low wavenumbers). It then cascades
  through the inertial range and is removed by viscosity at the small
  scales — a steady statistical balance rather than a decaying transient.
- **Reynolds number.** The Taylor-microscale Reynolds number is
  $\mathrm{Re}_\lambda \approx 433$, well into the turbulent regime, giving
  a clear inertial range in which to look for the $-5/3$ law.

The full database stores thousands of snapshots in time. For this course we
use a **manageable extract** — a $200^3$ sub-cube of the domain (and, for
the time-history exercises, a record of several hundred snapshots at
selected points) — so that everything runs comfortably in a notebook on the
cluster rather than needing a supercomputer.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why HIT is the right first dataset

Because HIT has no mean flow and no walls, the **fluctuations are the whole
signal**: a Reynolds decomposition $u_i = \langle u_i\rangle + u_i'$ has
$\langle u_i\rangle \approx 0$, so $u_i' \approx u_i$. That lets you focus
on the statistics themselves — variances, two-point correlations, spectra —
without first having to subtract a complicated mean profile. You will add
that complication later, with wall-bounded flows.
:::

## Where the data lives

On the course cluster the extracted field is stored at:

```bash
/project/60004/00_Assignment1/isotropic.parquet
```

You do **not** need to download it or copy it into your home directory —
read it in place from your notebook. In Python:

```{python}
#| eval: false
import pandas as pd

path = "/project/60004/00_Assignment1/isotropic.parquet"
df = pd.read_parquet(path)      # needs pyarrow (or fastparquet)
print(df.shape)
df.head()
```

Each row is one sample; the columns are the coordinates
`x, y, z`, the three velocity components `velocity_x, velocity_y,
velocity_z`, and a `Timestep` index for the time-history points. Because
Parquet is *columnar* (see below), you can even read just the columns you
need — for example only the velocities — without loading the whole file.

## A note on file formats: what is Parquet?

Scientific data is rarely stored as plain text `.csv` for anything large —
CSV is slow to parse, stores every number as human-readable characters
(wasteful), and keeps no type information. **Apache Parquet** (`.parquet`)
is one of several *binary, high-performance* formats built to fix that.
Its key properties:

- **Columnar.** Values are stored column-by-column, not row-by-row. All the
  $u_x$ values sit together, then all the $u_y$, and so on. This means you
  can read *only the columns you need* (say, the velocities) and skip the
  rest — a huge saving when a file has many columns.
- **Compressed.** Each column is a run of same-typed numbers, which
  compresses extremely well (Snappy, ZSTD, gzip). A Parquet file is
  typically several times smaller than the equivalent CSV.
- **Typed.** The schema (column names and data types) is stored *inside*
  the file. `float64` stays `float64`; there is no guessing or re-parsing
  when you read it back.
- **Fast and portable.** It is the storage format of the Apache Arrow
  ecosystem and is read natively by pandas, Polars, Dask, and Spark, so the
  same file works across tools and languages.

### Other formats you will meet

Parquet is excellent for *tabular* data (rows and columns). Turbulence data
is often naturally an **N-dimensional array** — a $200^3$ velocity field is
really a 4-D array (three space indices, plus the component). Different
formats specialise in that:

- **HDF5** (`.h5`, read with `h5py`) — the workhorse for scientific
  N-dimensional arrays. It stores multiple datasets and metadata in one
  file in a filesystem-like hierarchy and supports **partial (sliced)
  reads**, so you can pull one 2-D plane out of a huge 3-D field without
  loading all of it. Most DNS and CFD codes write HDF5.
- **NetCDF** — widely used in climate and geophysical fluid dynamics; a
  self-describing, HDF5-based format with rich metadata conventions.
- **Zarr** — like HDF5 but *chunked and cloud-native*: arrays are split into
  many small pieces that can be read in parallel and streamed from object
  storage (S3, etc.). Well suited to very large fields and cluster
  workflows.
- **Feather / Arrow IPC** — the in-memory Arrow format written to disk;
  extremely fast for handing tables between processes, though less
  compressed than Parquet for long-term storage.

The common thread: all of these are **binary, typed, and support
compression and partial reads** — which is what makes working with
multi-gigabyte turbulence fields practical. For the tabular extract in this
assignment, **Parquet** is the natural choice; when you later work with raw
3-D snapshots, expect **HDF5**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reading only what you need

Because Parquet is columnar, you can ask for specific columns at read time:

```{python}
#| eval: false
# read only the velocity columns — coordinates are skipped on disk
u = pd.read_parquet(path, columns=["velocity_x", "velocity_y", "velocity_z"])
```

This is the columnar advantage in one line: less I/O, less memory, faster
load.
:::
